cards.front: Recall a key point about Political Parties & Government
cards.back: Conservative Party: centre-right, supports free market capitalism, low taxes, private enterprise, traditional values, and strong defence. Traditionally supported by business owners, middle-class and older voters. Key policies: lower taxation, privatisation, strong law and order.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Political Parties & Government
cards.back: Labour Party: centre-left, supports social justice, public services, workers' rights, and redistribution of wealth through taxation. Traditionally supported by working-class voters, trade unions and ethnic minorities. Key policies: NHS investment, higher minimum wage, nationalisation of key services.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Political Parties & Government
cards.back: Other parties: Liberal Democrats (centre, proportional representation, civil liberties, EU membership), Green Party (environmentalism, social justice, renewable energy), Reform UK (right-wing populist, Eurosceptic, lower immigration, lower tax), Scottish National Party (Scottish independence, centre-left social democracy), Plaid Cymru (Welsh interests).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Political Parties & Government
cards.back: How government is formed: after a general election, the leader of the party with the most MPs usually becomes Prime Minister. If no party has a majority (hung parliament), parties negotiate to form a coalition (Conservative-Lib Dem 2010-2015) or a minority government with confidence-and-supply agreements. The PM appoints the Cabinet (about 20 senior ministers who run government departments).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Political Parties & Government
cards.back: The Prime Minister's powers: appoints and dismisses Cabinet ministers, chairs Cabinet, leads the governing party, represents the UK internationally, and can call early elections (with 2/3 Commons majority or via no-confidence vote). The PM is NOT directly elected by the public - they become PM by being leader of the largest party in the Commons.

cards.front: What should you know about citizenship studies exam tips — political parties & government?
cards.back: 1. For Political Parties & Government questions, use citizenship terminology and reference democratic processes accurately 2. Consider multiple viewpoints — including those you disagree with 3. Link Political Parties & Government to current affairs and real-world examples where possible 4. When evaluating, consider both rights and responsibilities 5. Structure longer answers: identify the issue, analyse different perspectives, reach a justified view
Evaluate whether the UK's system of forming a government is democratic.

cards.back: Political Parties & Government is a core topic in GCSE Citizenship Studies that requires understanding of how the UK political and legal systems work, and how citizens can participate effectively. The specification requires you to know how British democracy functions, understand your rights and responsibilities as a citizen, and be able to take informed and responsible action on citizenship issues

cards.front: Political Parties & Government and UK Democratic Processes
cards.back: The UK is a parliamentary democracy where citizens exercise power through elected representatives. Understanding political parties & government requires knowledge of how democratic processes work: general elections (first past the post), devolved elections (additional member system for Scotland and Wales), local elections, and referendums. cards.front: Rights, Responsibilities and Political Parties & Government
cards.back: UK citizens have both rights and responsibilities. Key rights include: the right to vote, freedom of speech, freedom of religion, the right to a fair trial, and the right to privacy. These rights are protected by the Human Rights Act 1998, which incorporates the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law.
